title: What Depression-era music jobs paid
summary: Breaux gives matinee and night-dance pay at the Tick Tock and general Depression prices, then they stray into Nicholson and other bandleaders.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: The Depression years and the WPA band

blocks.x: How much did you get paid, say, with Clyde Carr's band? Practically nothing?

You know, I think it's something people ought to know about the Depression. Well, for the matinee, you got, I think the matinee at that time was paying six bits, sometime a dollar. The night dance was down a quarter. Unless there didn't be a special dance, some club or another, well then you could squeeze out maybe a down half, maybe two dollars.
Well, how much were music jobs paying generally during the Depression?

During the Depression generally? Yeah. Down a quarter was the top price, most places. Yeah. I mean, now and then you get a special affair for two dollars a night. Oh, I know you know Sam Nicholson. Oh, yeah. Sam and his brother. Well, uh... Get the whole player. Phillip. Phillip. Phillip. Well, listen, it's just, those Nicholson, I mean, I knew them not too very well, but they related to Albert Nichols. No, no. Because Albert Nicholson was... That was Nicholson. Oh, Nicholson. Sam Nicholson. And, uh... His brother...
Nickerson and his brother, he did talk with his college man. That was Nickerson.

I don't know what Jimmy Jolison. I don't know, I don't know, uh, Mac Neal, the Sonny South, Mac Neal, Sonny South. He was a fine trumpet man. He had a nice band too. I used to, I used to hear that most like the, uh, the San Jacinto quote. Bob lines? No, I didn't know him too well.
